Screens: sign-in ("Sign in with your staff key", the browser's prompt, errors in the words of section 10); home (signed in as, role, the staff sign-ins of every staff account in the last 7 days (time and handle, newest first, read page by page until a sign-in older than 7 days), the session's absolute end ("Signed in until 21:40"), the person's staff sessions with "Sign out that session" confirmed by the key, the person's keys); the audit log (a table, newest first, "Load older", and "Go to place", which opens the page at a place the keeper kept); "Cases arrive in sub-project 3c." When `GET /api/staff/me` answers 404, the console shows only "The staff console is not available at this address. It is off on this server, or this is not the address set in CONSOLE_ORIGIN: open it at exactly that address, never at 127.0.0.1." The staff gate answers a wrong Host with the same 404 as a console that is off, so the page cannot tell the two apart.

Before it asks for the key to confirm an action, the console checks the step-up options it was given. The challenge must be the 74 bytes of the step-up layout (the contracts' offsets) with the `staff_step_up` purpose, its binding must equal the sha256 of the session's handle (from `GET /api/staff/me`), a newline and the action's hash that the page computes with WebCrypto from the `{ action, target, params }` it sent, and the allow list must hold one key. Otherwise the page does not call `navigator.credentials.get` and says the confirmation could not be checked. So an API under an attacker's control cannot have the key sign an action the person did not choose; the check trusts the page, which Caddy serves from its image, not the API.

Enrolment. Before the ceremony the page says which keys work: a security key with a PIN, or Windows Hello on this computer. It says which will be refused: passkeys saved by a password manager, such as iCloud Keychain or Google Password Manager, and a phone's own passkeys. It says how to set a PIN on a new security key when the browser does not offer to. It asks for the key's name, and says the key will show that name, so it should not be an email or a real name. It offers two buttons. "Register a security key" sends `kind: security_key`. "Use Windows Hello on this computer" sends `kind: this_device`, and the page says to choose Windows Hello or this device in the browser's dialog. Each refusal is explained in words: `staff_key_not_device_bound` means the browser saved a synced passkey, `staff_key_not_user_verified` means the key asked for no PIN or fingerprint, and `staff_key_refused` means the browser's answer could not be checked. The page says the link still works. After either of the first two refusals, and only when the enrolment options say that the console's relying party ID is not the app's (`rpShared` false), the page calls `PublicKeyCredential.signalUnknownCredential({ rpId, credentialId })` for the credential it has just created, where the browser has the call (Chrome and Edge 132+, Safari 26), so the password manager drops the refused passkey. Where the browser lacks the call, or the two IDs are shared, the page tells the person to delete the console's entry from their password manager by hand. The WebKit bugs that kept 1c from the Signal API (322267 and 302624) delete other passkeys only on the same relying party ID, and outside development the console's ID holds no synced passkey that korbat accepts; in development both IDs are `localhost`, where the call could delete the developer's app passkeys, so the page does not make it there. Sign-in never calls it, because every failure before the signature gets one answer. A failed sign-in says to choose the security key or Windows Hello rather than a password manager's passkey.

The console sends `X-Staff-Activity: 1` on every request a person's action starts, and on no other. Its only timed requests are the two reads of its idle timer, which carry no mark. The timer restarts at 15 minutes, or at the time left to the session's absolute end when that is less, whenever an activity-marked request succeeds. Two minutes before it runs out (at 13 minutes of a full idle period) the console reads `GET /api/staff/me`: when more than two minutes are left (the person acted in another tab of the same session), it sets the timer from the answer's seconds left; otherwise it shows, in a live region, "Your staff session ends in 2 minutes." with a "Stay signed in" button that sends one activity-marked `GET /api/staff/me`. When the absolute end is the nearer one, the warning instead reads "Your staff session ends at 21:40. Sign in again with your staff key then." and has no button, since nothing moves the absolute end. When the timer runs out it reads `/me` once more and either sets the timer from the answer or shows sign-in. Any `staff_session_required` answer shows the sign-in screen in place with "Your staff session ended" and keeps the path; after the sign-in the console returns to that path. A later screen that refreshes itself (3c's queue) sends its refreshes without the mark, and 3c keeps a draft in memory across a sign-in by the same account.

The build writes `dist/index.html` and hashed bundle and stylesheet files; esbuild's options pin the target and minify.

## 10. Contracts

`packages/contracts/src/staff.ts` holds: the enrolment, sign-in and step-up requests and answers (WebAuthn JSON through the existing schemas; the enrolment options request is `{ token, name, kind }`, with `kind` one of `security_key` and `this_device`, and its answer also says whether the console's relying party ID is the app's (`rpShared`); the step-up options request is `{ action, target, params }`); `STAFF_STEP_UP_ACTIONS`, each step-up action's name, target type and the zod schema of its params, read by the step-up options, `requireStaffStepUp`, `audit-verify` and the console (3a: `staff_session_revoked`, a staff session as target, params `{}`); the action's sorted-JSON text and the step-up challenge's layout (its offsets and purpose code), which the API, `audit-verify` and the console share; the stored assertion's shape; `StaffMe` (with the session's handle, `idleSecondsLeft` and `absoluteSecondsLeft`), `StaffSession` (with `browser`), `StaffKey`, `AuditEntry` and `AuditPage` (with the `at` request); and `StaffErrorCode`.

`StaffErrorCode` lists `staff_session_required`, `staff_key_invalid`, `staff_key_suspended`, `staff_key_limit`, `staff_key_not_device_bound`, `staff_key_not_user_verified`, `staff_key_refused`, `staff_enrollment_invalid`, `staff_step_up_required` and `staff_step_up_invalid`. `staff_key_invalid` covers an unknown or revoked key, an account that is no longer live or staff, a sign-in challenge the codec refuses and a response the library refuses, with one answer for all. The auth module raises these codes: `AuthErrorKind` becomes `AuthErrorCode | StaffErrorCode | "invalid_request"`, and `MESSAGES` (`apps/api/src/auth/context.ts`) gains their messages, so `app.ts`'s error handler needs no new branch. Staff routes may also answer the shared `challenge_expired`, `rate_limited` and `invalid_request`, and the staff gate's `not_found` and `csrf_failed`. They never answer a `passkey_*` code, whose messages send people to remedies the console does not have: the staff flows catch the codec's and the wrapper's `passkey_invalid` and `passkey_unsupported` and raise `staff_key_invalid` at sign-in, `staff_step_up_invalid` at step-up and `staff_key_refused` at enrolment. Where only the operator can help, the messages say so.

- `staff_session_required`: "Your staff session ended. Sign in with your staff key."
- `staff_key_invalid`: "This key does not open the staff console. If it should, ask the operator to check your staff keys."
- `staff_key_suspended`: "This staff key was switched off because a copy of it may exist. Ask the operator for a link to enrol a new one."
- `staff_key_limit`: "This account has 5 staff keys. Ask the operator to revoke one before enrolling another."
- `staff_key_not_device_bound`: "This key can be synced or copied, so it cannot be a staff key. Use a security key or a device-bound authenticator."
- `staff_key_not_user_verified`: "This key did not ask for a PIN or fingerprint, so it cannot be a staff key. Set a PIN on it, or use another key."
- `staff_key_refused`: "The browser's answer for this key could not be checked. Try again, or use another key; this link still works."
- `staff_enrollment_invalid`: "This enrolment link has expired or was already used. Ask the operator for a new one."
- `staff_step_up_required`: "Confirm this with your staff key."
- `staff_step_up_invalid`: "That confirmation was for another action, was already used or could not be checked. Try again."

The console words every code it can receive from a table of its own, using these texts.

## 11. Security and privacy

What stays impossible even for an admin, and what proves it (`threats.md` 3.3.1): no route changes a role (a route-table test); no route acts as another user or reads another user's sessions, email, IP, device or phone (a route-table test and the architecture rule); no audit row can be changed, removed or placed out of the chain by the API role (database tests: UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE on `audit_log`; any write to or lock on `audit_head`; `session_replication_role`; disabling the trigger; a temporary `audit_head`; an insert naming an existing id; supplied chain columns), and a change by the owner `korbat_migrate` or the superuser to rows a kept head covers is detected by `audit-verify` against that head; no staff power without a staff session, on the console's origin, from a staff key whose authenticator reported UV and no BE (integration tests with the software authenticator, including a key reporting BE refused at enrolment and at sign-in, a key reporting no UV refused, a response without the owner's user handle refused, a personal passkey refused, an assertion from the app's origin refused, an app session cookie refused, a bearer token refused); no staff answer readable or actionable from another origin: staff routes carry no CORS headers, the staff gate refuses a foreign Origin or a `Sec-Fetch-Site` other than same-origin on every method, and the configuration refuses the console's origin in the app's trusted origins (HTTP and configuration tests); no action confirmed by an assertion made for another (a step-up test), and no key asked to sign a step-up whose challenge binds another action than the one the person chose (the console's tests and the browser check); no staff key or staff session left live, and no unused enrolment left, after a demotion or a deletion, and no key enrolled by a link issued before a `revoke ... all`, a demotion or a deletion (integration tests); no page left open keeping a staff session past 15 minutes without an action by its person (an integration test and the console's timer tests). No staff key exists without an enrolment the command line issued, and no code in the API can add one, delete one or revive a revoked or suspect one (database tests as `korbat_auth`). No row of a step-up action is in the record, whatever its actor, without an assertion that `audit-verify` checks against a key of that row's actor (audit tests), and no staff session pairs an account with another account's key (a database test). Every auth-side fact commits or rolls back together with its audit row (an audit test). Rows without a step-up, such as sign-ins and sign-outs, remain the API's word.

What the flags cannot prove: without attestation, UV and BE are claims the authenticator makes about itself, so a software authenticator that reports BE=0 while its key can be copied would pass. That residual is left to three things. The runbook lists the authenticators staff use: a FIDO2 security key with a PIN, or Windows Hello on a computer with a TPM. The operator hands over each enrolment link. `staff.js keys` prints each key's reported AAGUID, which is zeros when the browser or the authenticator withholds it.

Staff keys are never shown in full; the audit reader never returns metadata that names a person beyond the actor's handle.

## 12. Testing

- **Unit**: configuration refinements (`CONSOLE_ORIGIN` blank counts as unset; it is refused in every environment when it equals `APP_ORIGIN` or appears in `TRUSTED_ORIGINS`; in production it is refused on the app's hostname with another port, and when the app's hostname is a subdomain of it; the production rules for the console's relying party, which do not apply outside production); `chain.ts`'s canonical text and hash against a fixed set of test vectors (rows with nulls, empty strings, quotes, backslashes, control characters, non-ASCII text, nested metadata and a step-up, each with its metadata text, expected canonical text and hash), which the integration parity test also inserts; the action's hash (sorted JSON of action, target and params) and the step-up binding; the step-up challenge (sealing, the binding, expiry); the codec's staff purposes: each is refused for any other purpose, an app sign-in challenge is refused at the console's sign-in and the reverse, `staff_register` is refused for another enrolment, and `staff_step_up` is refused for another session, action, target or params (in 3a the params binding is tested here: its one step-up action has params `{}`, so other params never reach the binding in an integration test); the staff gate on a Hono app with a stub route behind it (Host, Origin and `Sec-Fetch-Site`); the wrapper's options carry `userVerification: "required"` only when asked, and 1c's callers still get `"preferred"`; the security-key hint is sent only when asked; the console's pure parts (the router, the answer parsing); source scans: no HTML sinks in `apps/admin`, zod jitless, the staff module importing neither an auth-schema table nor `createAuthRepo` or `createSessions` (the architecture test's rules, each with a test that catches a deliberate violation); a source scan that the console's development server sends the same CSP as the Caddyfile's console site.
- **Integration (auth side)**: the staff harness runs the console at `http://console.localhost:8090` (relying party `console.localhost`) beside the app at `http://localhost:8081` (`localhost`). Enrolment (token single-use, expiry, staff only, an account without a handle, user verification required, a key without UV refused with `staff_key_not_user_verified` while the link still works, backup-eligible refused, a response the library refuses answered `staff_key_refused` while the link still works, an enrolment recorded for another origin refused, the key stored with its enrolment's origin and relying party ID, five keys at most and a sixth refused with `staff_key_limit`, excludeCredentials; the options' user handle is the account's `webauthn_user_id`, set when it is absent, and their user name and display name are the key's name); the database's refusals (as `korbat_auth`, INSERT into `staff_keys` and `staff_enrollments`, DELETE from `staff_keys`, UPDATE of a key's `public_key`, and clearing `revoked_at`, `suspect_at` or `used_at` fail; `auth.add_staff_key` refuses an unknown, spent or expired token, a token hash given in place of the token, a demoted or deleted account and a sixth key; `auth.forget_staff_keys` changes nothing for a live account; a staff session row lasting beyond 12 hours, or pairing an account with another account's key, is refused by the database); sign-in (a live staff key only, a response without a user handle or with another account's refused, user verification required, an assertion without UV or with BE or BS refused after the signature, a revoked key, a demoted account, a deleted account, ten unsigned responses naming a key's credential id leaving its owner able to sign in); the counter rule (a regression at sign-in and at step-up revokes the key and every staff session it opened, the current one included, and writes `staff_key_counter_regression`, its audit row and the `staff_key_suspect` mail); relying parties (a staff-key assertion made for the app's relying party and a personal-passkey assertion made for the console's are both refused on the relying-party check; one test runs with both relying party IDs `localhost`, the development configuration, and shows that the tables alone refuse a personal passkey at the console and a staff key at the app, and that each kind's registration options then exclude the account's credentials of the other kind); sessions (idle and absolute limits with the clock; an unmarked request that neither slides the idle expiry nor moves `last_used_at`, so a session read only by unmarked requests ends 15 minutes after the last marked one; a marked request that slides it, never past the absolute expiry; a revocation, a suspect key, a demotion and a take-down each refused at the session's next request; the stored browser label; the cookies' flags and their 12-hour Max-Age; both cookies cleared on `staff_session_required`; the host and origin checks; CSRF); lifecycle (grant-role to `user` revokes every staff key and staff session and deletes unused enrolments, and a later grant back to staff revives no key; a change between `moderator` and `admin` revokes staff sessions and enrolments and keeps keys; `revoke ... all` deletes unused enrolments and writes `staff_enrollments_cancelled`; an enrolment verified after `revoke ... all`, a demotion or a deletion enrols nothing; the take-down revokes the account's staff keys and staff sessions, deletes its enrolments, blanks its keys' names, AAGUIDs and transports, and writes its audit rows after `account_deleted`, in `takeDown` and in `finishTakeDown`; the janitor deletes staff sessions 30 days after they end and enrolments a day after use or expiry, and never a live one); mails (each of the four staff mails sent where section 7 says and nowhere else; `revoke ... all` on an account with only an unused enrolment writes `staff_enrollments_cancelled` and mails nothing; a counter regression appends `staff_key_counter_regression` and mails `staff_key_suspect`, never `passkey_suspect`; the templates pinned in `apps/api/test/mail/templates.test.ts`, none containing a URL); step-up (bound to action and target, single use, expiry, the wrong key, the counter rule; the params binding is a unit test in 3a, above).
- **Integration (audit)**: every staff action writes one row with the chain. Parity: rows with the test vectors' contents, written through the trigger from a session with a non-UTC `TimeZone` and `DateStyle` 'SQL, DMY', recompute in `chain.ts` to the stored hashes. Concurrency: several sessions insert at once, some inside transactions, and `audit-verify`, run while they insert and again after, passes walking `chain_seq`. An insert naming an existing id with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` is written under a new id and chained; supplied `id`, `created_at`, `chain_version`, `chain_seq`, `prev_hash` and `hash` are overwritten; a temporary `audit_head` that `korbat_api` creates changes nothing. `korbat_api` cannot UPDATE, DELETE or TRUNCATE `audit_log`, nor write or lock `audit_head`, set `session_replication_role` or disable the trigger. With the head row missing, an insert fails with `the audit head is missing`. As the owner `korbat_migrate` (the test environment has no superuser URL): a row changed alone fails a plain `audit-verify`; a row changed with every later hash and the head recomputed passes a plain one and fails against a pair kept before the change. Every audit test that writes a row `audit-verify` must refuse runs inside one transaction that ends in a rollback and hands that transaction to the verifier's check, so no later file sees a broken chain: the parity rows (their step-up is signed by no stored key), the rows changed as the owner, a step-up action's row without an assertion, a key without its `staff_key_added` row and the missing head. Fixtures create staff keys only through the enrolment flow and `auth.add_staff_key`, and step-up rows only through the step-up flow. `global-setup.ts` inserts the head row `(1, 0, 64 zeros)` as `korbat_migrate` right after its truncate. Each auth-side fact's audit row commits and rolls back with its change (an error thrown after `auth.append_audit` leaves neither); `auth.append_audit` refuses an action outside its list; `audit-verify` passes a genuine step-up, with `CONSOLE_ORIGIN` unset too, and fails, naming the step-up check, when the row's params, target or session are changed as the owner or the assertion is moved to another row, each with every later hash and the head recomputed as in the rewrite test, when a row of a step-up action carries no assertion (under a staff, a demoted or the system actor), and when the assertion's key belongs to another account; it fails when a key has no `staff_key_added` row; grant-role's change and row are one transaction. The back-fill of 0012 is checked by the dry run, since the integration database holds no row older than 0012 (`scripts/test-db.mjs` migrates it and `global-setup.ts` then truncates every table): the dry run migrates the scratch database, which holds grant-role rows written before 0012, and runs `staff.js audit-verify` on it, which must pass.
- **HTTP**: the staff routes through the app with both origins configured: 404 with the console off; the app's session cookie and a bearer token refused on staff routes; a staff cookie refused on the app's routes; the no-store header; a console POST (the console's Host and Origin, the staff CSRF header) sent with the app's session and CSRF cookies present reaches the staff route and is not answered `csrf_failed`; no answer under `/api/staff/` carries an `Access-Control-*` header, even to an Origin listed in `TRUSTED_ORIGINS`; a GET with `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site` or `cross-site`, or with an Origin other than `CONSOLE_ORIGIN`, is refused and leaves the session's idle expiry unchanged; a request with another Host answers 404; the route table holds no route of another module under `/api/staff`; at enrolment, sign-in and step-up, a spent challenge, a challenge of another purpose, one with another binding and a response with a bad signature each answer a staff code, never a `passkey_*` one, and at sign-in a bad signature on a live key and an unknown key get the same answer; `GET /api/staff/audit?at=` answers the page whose newest row is at that place. The integration client's `Browser` (`apps/api/test/integration/http-client.ts`, which today always echoes into `x-csrf-token`, `:40-41`) takes, besides its origin, a base URL and the names of the CSRF cookie it echoes and of the header it echoes it in. It requests `base + path` and sends the base's host as `Host`, since behind Caddy `@hono/node-server` builds the request's URL from the Host header. A console client therefore carries the console's host and origin and echoes `__Host-korbat_staff_csrf` in `x-staff-csrf`; the existing clients keep `http://localhost` and echo `__Host-korbat_csrf` in `x-csrf-token`.
- **Console**: server-rendered checks of each screen and source scans, as the app's tests do; the idle timer with a fake clock (restart on a marked success, the read at 13 minutes, another tab's activity moving the end, the warning and "Stay signed in", the timer set to the absolute end when that is nearer and its warning without the button, sign-in in place on 401 returning to the path); the fetch wrapper sends the activity mark only when a caller asks for it; the check of step-up options (a challenge of another length or purpose, a binding for another action, target, params or session handle, and an allow list of more than one key, each refused before `navigator.credentials.get`); the home screen reading sign-ins back to 7 days; "Go to place"; the Signal API call made only when `rpShared` is false. A browser check is committed with the console (`apps/admin/test/browser/`, run by `pnpm --filter @korbat/admin test:browser`). It builds the console. A small Node server then serves `dist` with the headers of Caddy's console site, the CSP read from `infra/caddy/Caddyfile` so the two cannot drift. The same server answers `/api/staff/*` from fixtures whose user-written strings are hostile: markup, `javascript:` URLs, bidirectional overrides and the longest names allowed. The check drives Chromium through playwright-core with a CDP virtual authenticator (device-bound and user-verifying) over every screen: enrolment, sign-in, home, a session revoked with the key, a step-up whose options bind another action refused before the key is asked, the audit log and the ended session. It fails on any `securitypolicyviolation` event, any CSP or Trusted Types console message, any DevTools CSP issue, any page error and any dialog (the channels of `console-lab.md` section 2). It needs no database and writes nothing, so CI runs it with the runner's own Chrome and the dry run runs it on each build. 3c adds its screens and payloads to it. The dry run also walks the console against the scratch stack: an enrolment with the virtual authenticator set to backup-eligible, refused and explained, after which the same link from the command line enrols a device-bound key; sign-in; sessions listed; one revoked with the key; and the audit log read. That walk-through stays in the scratch tooling, since it writes to the database it runs against.
- **Smoke**: the smoke test takes `--console <url>`, required like `--base`. The console's page answers with the exact CSP and `Cache-Control: no-store, no-transform`, and `/api/staff/me` answers 404 on the app's host and 401 `staff_session_required` on the console's.

## 14. Success criteria

1. Nothing gives staff powers but a staff session on the console's origin from a staff key whose authenticator reported UV and no BE, and every test in section 11's list passes.
2. Staff keys exist only through enrolments the command line issued, which the database enforces; keys are revoked from the command line (`staff.js revoke` or a demotion by grant-role), by an account's take-down, or by a counter regression, which also marks them suspect; and every enrolment issued or cancelled, key, sign-in, sign-out, revocation and role change is in the audit log, written in the same transaction as its change.
3. The audit log is a hash chain the API role can only extend, in an order and at times the database alone sets; `audit-verify` recomputes it in its own code, and a change made by any role, the owner and the superuser included, to a row at or before a kept head is detected when `audit-verify` runs with that head; and every row of a step-up action in it carries an assertion that `audit-verify` checks against the public key of a key its actor holds.
4. The console runs under the strict policy of section 3 with no violation in the committed browser check of section 12, over every screen with hostile fixtures, and renders every user string as text.
5. The app is unchanged for everyone but staff, whose staff powers are gone from it.

## 15. Amendments from the dry run (2026-10-01)

Found while the tasks were dry-run in the scratch clone, by the conformance review of each task, by the adversarial review of the range and by a walk-through in a real browser; each is applied in the prompts. Where an amendment and a section above differ, the amendment is current.

- **"Has a handle" is the auth side's record (section 6, `auth.add_staff_key`).** The function checks `auth.users.onboarded_at is not null`, which onboarding sets right after the profile and its handle exist; it never reads `public.profiles`.
- **One policy per staff table (section 6).** Each auth staff table has one `FOR ALL` policy for `korbat_auth`; a single narrower policy cannot serve the reads, updates and deletes the role needs, and the grants do the restricting.
- **Set values stay set (section 6).** The never-cleared trigger refuses to clear or change a set `revoked_at`, `suspect_at` or `used_at`, so every revocation sets `revoked_at` only where it is still null; a check constraint, `staff_keys_suspect_is_revoked`, keeps `suspect_at` from being set without `revoked_at`.
- **`CONSOLE_ORIGIN` is written as a browser sends it (section 8).** Scheme, host and port only: lowercase, no path, no trailing slash, no default port, because the staff gate compares the `Origin` header with it as a string; equality with `APP_ORIGIN` and the `TRUSTED_ORIGINS` entries is judged by origin; production also refuses an IP address or `localhost` for the console, as for the app; a `CONSOLE_RP_ID` set while `CONSOLE_ORIGIN` is unset is kept.
- **The functions' answers (section 6).** `auth.add_staff_key` returns the key's id, `auth.append_audit` the row's `chain_seq`, and `auth.forget_staff_keys` how many keys it blanked; refusals raise the staff error code itself as the message (`staff_enrollment_invalid`, `staff_key_limit`), which the flows map; a `staff_key_added` row's metadata is `{"enrollmentId": ...}`, never the key's name or AAGUID.
- **Contracts the design left open (section 10).** `StaffEnrollVerifyResponse` is `{ key: StaffKey }`, `StaffSignInVerifyResponse` is `StaffMe`, `AuditPageQuery` refuses `cursor` and `at` together, `StaffMe` refuses an idle end later than the absolute end, and `STAFF_AUDIT_PAGE_SIZE` is 50.
- **Grant-role's first statement locks the account (section 7, Role changes).** It is a `SELECT ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE` of the account's row, which takes the same lock as the role's update, because the `role_granted` row needs the previous role, which `UPDATE ... RETURNING` does not give.
- **`audit-verify`'s session settings (section 7, Command line).** It sets `DateStyle` ISO, `TimeZone` UTC and the 10-second `lock_timeout` with `SET LOCAL` at the start of its verifying transaction, so the same check runs inside a transaction a test hands it (`checkAuditRecord(tx, kept, keysFrom)`, whose keys come from the auth role when the handed transaction is on the API's).
- **What `audit-verify` also refuses (section 7).** Rows at a place of 0 or below, rows beyond the head, and kept places that name no row.
- **Each command reads only its own settings (section 7).** `staff.js` never loads the API's configuration: `audit-head` reads `DATABASE_URL_API`, `audit-verify` that and `DATABASE_URL_AUTH`, each through a narrow schema (`staffDatabaseUrls`), so it runs with the console off, moved or misconfigured; `config.ts` exports the PostgreSQL URL rule both use.
- **Bundle entries never import each other (section 5).** In a bundle every module's `import.meta.url` is the bundle's, so an entry that imported another entry's file would run that entry's main too; the lock-timeout helpers live in `cli/lock-timeout.ts`, `SYSTEM_ACTOR_ID` moved to `auth/admin.ts`, and `build.mjs` says so.
- **The gate's answers (section 7, The staff gate).** Another Host gets the app's own unknown-route 404 (`c.notFound()`), compared exactly, without lowercasing; a failed Origin or `Sec-Fetch-Site` test is `AuthError("csrf_failed", 403)`.
- **The reader past the head (section 7, The audit log).** For an `at` beyond the head the reader returns the newest page.
- **Who the take-down's record names (section 7).** The account itself in `takeDown`, since its owner asked for the deletion, and the system actor in `finishTakeDown`, which the purge job runs; `finishTakeDown` now takes the account's row first with `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, as every writer of staff rows does.
- **The shapes of the staff record's rows (section 7).** `staff_key_revoked`: target `staff_key`, metadata `{ keyId, sessionsRevoked, via }`, `key_id` null; `staff_enrollments_cancelled`: target `user`, metadata `{ count, via }`; an enrolment issued by `staff.js enroll`: target `user`, metadata `{ enrollmentId, via: "cli" }`.
- **The take-down's enrolments (section 7).** It deletes every enrolment, spent ones too, and its `staff_enrollments_cancelled` row counts only the links that were still open, written only when there was one.
- **`staff.js keys` without an email (section 7).** It lists live accounts whose role is not `user`, and reads their handles on the API's role, so it needs both database URLs.
- **The command line's mailer (section 7).** `cli/mail.ts` builds it from `SMTP_URL` and `MAIL_FROM`; grant-role uses it, and its result gains the staff counts and `mailError`.
- **No limit of its own on enrolment (section 7).** The enrolment routes have only the global rate limit; the link's 30 minutes and single use bound them.
- **BS without BE is malformed (section 7, Sign-in).** @simplewebauthn/server 14.0.2 rejects an assertion that reports BS without BE before the flow sees its flags, so that case answers `staff_key_invalid`; BE, backed up or not, answers `staff_key_not_device_bound` as designed.
- **The marked read is an update (section 7, Every staff request).** A request marked `X-Staff-Activity: 1` reads and slides its session in one `UPDATE ... FROM` the staff keys joined to the users; the account is reached as the key's owner, which the sessions' foreign key on `(key_id, user_id)` makes the session's account.
- **An expired sign-in challenge (section 7, Sign-in).** It answers the shared `challenge_expired`, as enrolment does, which section 10 allows; forged, other-purpose and spent challenges answer `staff_key_invalid`.
- **The sign-in record's shapes (section 7).** `staff_sign_in` and `staff_signed_out` rows: the account as actor, the session as target (`staff_session`, its handle), the handle and the key in their columns, metadata `{}`; their auth events carry `{ keyId, handle }` and `{ handle }`; `staff_key_counter_regression`: the key's owner as actor, the key as target, metadata `{ keyId, sessionsRevoked, via }`.
- **What the console reads (section 7, Sessions and keys).** `GET /api/staff/keys` lists live keys only, since `StaffKey` has no revoked field; sign-in options have only the global rate limit.
- **`staff.js revoke`'s edges (section 7, Command line).** An already revoked key exits 0 having written nothing and mailed nothing, and so does `all` with nothing left; an unknown account, or a key that is unknown or another account's, exits 1; it reads `DATABASE_URL_AUTH`, `SMTP_URL`, `MAIL_FROM` and `NODE_ENV` only.
- **The step-up middleware validates the body (section 7, Step-up).** `requireStaffStepUp` validates the action's strict params with an optional `stepUp` through the shared validator, so a missing assertion answers `staff_step_up_required` rather than `invalid_request`; the route reads the confirmed result from `staffStepUp`.
- **Status codes (sections 7 and 10).** `staff_step_up_required` and `staff_step_up_invalid` answer 403; a handle that names no live session of the person's own answers `404 not_found` ("No such session"), as the app's own session revocation does.
- **The re-check before the action (section 7, Step-up).** The revocation's transaction locks the account's row, then checks that the confirming key and the account are still live, answering `staff_session_required` and writing nothing otherwise; a person may revoke the session they confirm from.
- **Lower-case targets (section 10).** A step-up target id is PostgreSQL's lower-case uuid only (`LowerCaseUuid`); any other spelling is refused with `invalid_request`, because the record hashes the target exactly as confirmed and stores the database's form.
- **`staff_session_required` clears the cookies wherever it is raised (section 7).** `requireStaff` checks `c.error` after `next()`, since Hono hands an error thrown behind it to `app.onError`, and clears both staff cookies on the answer.
- **A step-up challenge needs a minute left (section 7, Step-up).** It carries the full 10 minutes, but is read only while more than one minute is left (`STEP_UP_READ_MARGIN_MS`), so a confirmed row is never written after the expiry `audit-verify` checks; the margin assumes the API's and the database's clocks agree.
- **What `audit-verify` also checks (section 7).** That the stored `action_hash` equals the recomputed one, and it reports a challenge used twice as its own problem; it does not check `metadata.params` against the action's schema.
- **The console's type declarations (section 9).** There is no `@types/react-dom` in the lockfile, so `src/react-dom.d.ts` declares `react-dom/client` and `react-dom/server`, as the app's tests do; `@types/react` 19.2.18 and `@types/node` 24.13.5, both already locked, are its devDependencies.
- **"Your staff session ended" (section 9).** It shows when the page held a session, or when the refused request carried the staff CSRF cookie (read before sending, since the 401 clears it), so a reload or a new tab after an idle end says so too; a 401 with neither (never signed in, signed out, past the cookie's 12 hours) shows plain sign-in.
- **The home screen's 7 days (section 9).** Opening Home does one marked `GET /api/staff/me` and counts the 7 days back from that answer's server time, not from the session read at sign-in.
- **The console's own checks (section 9).** The step-up check also checks the challenge's version byte, and every ceremony forces user verification "required", attestation "none" and no extension but `credProps`, whatever the server's options say; the staff CSRF header goes on every request while the cookie exists.
- **The console site's headers live in `apps/admin/site-headers.mjs` (sections 8 and 9).** The development server uses them; Task 7's Caddyfile and the scan that compares them must match.
- **The app's site refuses staff paths with two handles (section 8).** Caddy 2.11.4 sorts `handle` blocks by their path's length and compares paths only when a handle matches exactly one, so one handle matching both `/api/staff` and `/api/staff/*` is not reliably placed ahead of `handle /api/*`; two one-path handles, longer than `/api/*`, always are. The refusal is a shared snippet that answers the API's error envelope without a request id, which is how the smoke test tells Caddy's answer from the API's.
- **`immutable` only on real build files (section 8).** The console site's hashed-file rule adds Caddy's `file` condition to `path /assets/*`, so the `index.html` fallback served for a missing hashed name keeps `no-store, no-transform`.
- **The browser check's reach (section 12).** Beyond the screens section 12 lists, it covers an unknown address, sign-out and the enrolment refusal of a synced passkey; CI runs it with `KORBAT_BROWSER_CHANNEL=chrome`.
- **Every ceremony's challenge is checked before the key is asked (sections 5, 9 and 11; found by the review).** The contracts export the 58-byte layout (`CEREMONY_CHALLENGE`) and every purpose code (`CHALLENGE_PURPOSES`) beside `STAFF_STEP_UP_CHALLENGE`, and the codec reads them from there. Before every `navigator.credentials` call the console checks the challenge: at sign-in 58 bytes, version 1, purpose `staff_signin` and a zero binding; at enrolment 58 bytes, version 1, purpose `staff_register` (its binding names the enrolment, which the page is never told, so it cannot be checked there); at step-up the 74-byte check. No key is asked at sign-in or enrolment to sign another ceremony's challenge.
- **`audit-verify` reads every row (section 7, Command line; found by the review).** It pages on `(chain_seq, id)` and, in the same snapshot, fails on a place held by two rows, a row with no place, or a row count that does not equal the rows read plus the rows beyond the head.
- **Keys are judged by where they were enrolled (sections 2 and 7; found by the review).** A key whose recorded origin or relying party ID differs from the running configuration is `staff_key_invalid` at sign-in, before the signature, and `staff_step_up_invalid` at the step-up's options and confirmation; assertions are verified against the key's recorded values. Moving the console means enrolling every key again, and the API enforces it.
- **The enrolment page signs in with the new key itself (sections 2 and 9; found by the review).** Its "Sign in with this key" button narrows the allowed credentials to the key just registered and signs in whatever session the browser holds, so the check after each enrolment always uses the new key.
- **A confirmed action never lands after its expiry (sections 2 and 7; found by the review).** The confirmed revocation's transaction sets `lock_timeout` to the lesser of 15 seconds and a third of the challenge's remaining life by the database's clock, and the statement that writes its audit row reads the database's clock after the insert and undoes everything when the challenge has expired; a late confirmation writes nothing and answers `challenge_expired`. The one-minute read margin no longer assumes the API's and the database's clocks agree.
- **`auth.forget_staff_keys` blanks only revoked keys (section 6; found by the review).** Migration 0013 restates it so it blanks the name, AAGUID and transports only of keys whose `revoked_at` is set, of an account marked deleted; the take-down revokes them earlier in the same transaction, and code in the API gains nothing it cannot already do by revoking.
- **Revocation order and grant-role's after-commit steps (section 7, Role changes; found by the review).** Demotion and take-down revoke keys before staff sessions, as `staff.js revoke` does, so a concurrent sign-in cannot keep an unrevoked session; grant-role's cache tombstones and its mail run as independent best-effort steps after the commit, each reported as a warning, and the command exits 0 once the change is committed.
- **Smaller fixes (sections 7 and 9; found by the review).** `staff.js keys` reads in read-only transactions with a 10-second lock timeout; the console reads a marked `/me` right before the step-up options and every `/me` answer replaces the page's session; Go to place says when there is no row at the place asked for; an older Load older's answer never joins a page opened after it; the browser check's fixtures answer with the API's own statuses.

## 16. Changed by 3c (2026-10-09)

`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-02-moderation-cases-3c-design.md` (moderation cases) is the first work to stand on this foundation. It adds three step-up actions beside `staff_session_revoked` (`case_decided`, `appeals_reviewed` and `identity_revealed`, each a confirmed row that names its decision or its item), the console's queue, case page, composer and appeals, six commands of `staff.js` (`link`, `unlink`, `limits`, `text-verify`, `account-facts` and `access-request`), and staff mails that go to every staff account. What it changes in this document:

- **Three exceptions to the step-up rule (section 2, Confirming an action).** "A route that changes something asks for a fresh assertion" now has three named exceptions beside enrolment, sign-in, the step-up's own options and sign-out: saving a text (`POST /api/staff/cases/:case/texts`), taking a fresh snapshot (`POST /api/staff/cases/:case/snapshots`) and opening a finding (`POST /api/staff/findings`). None restricts or releases anything: a text enters the record only when a confirmed decision or reveal names its salted digest, and a finding is limited per staff account and day and counted on the home screen. The route-table test lists every changing route without a step-up by method and path.
- **"Followed only by deferred checks that read" (sections 6 and 7).** The rule that an audit row is always the last statement of its transaction becomes: followed only by deferred checks that read. A decision's audit row is written last by `append_confirmed_audit`, and at COMMIT the database's deferred constraint triggers hold the decision and every row of its ledger against that audit row; they take only ACCESS SHARE locks, which `korbat_api` cannot block, so the head's lock is still never held across a wait.
- **`ConsolePath` (section 9).** It becomes `"/" | "/audit" | "/signin" | "/queue" | "/appeals"`. The console gains one more address built from a value, a case's (`caseHref` over a `CaseId` that only `parseCaseId` makes, a lower-case uuid), written by `CaseLink` in `src/nav.tsx`, and one image site, `src/media.tsx`, whose address is built from two checked ids and a literal size; the source test pins both. Images reach the console only from its own origin, under the policy of section 8 unchanged.
- **The staff answers' new shapes (section 10).** The staff API gains the overview, the queue, a case, its images, snapshots and texts, the decision, the appeals and the review, and the reveal. No member of any answer is named like `email`, `address`, `userId`, `accountId` or `actorId`: people are handles, and a report's source is a summary in bands until a confirmed reveal. The route-table test's walk runs over the new answers and fails on a schema kind it does not read, and no staff route answers HEAD. The browser check gains the new screens with hostile fixtures, and the statuses a console request may meet gain 422 and 429.
- **`korbat_auth` can no longer clear or back-date `auth.users.deleted_at` (section 6, and the amendment on `auth.forget_staff_keys` in section 15).** Migration 0018's trigger `users_deleted_mark` makes a mark that `korbat_auth` sets the transaction's `now()` and refuses to clear or change one that is set. So the note in migration 0013 that `korbat_auth` may set and clear the mark is superseded; `auth.forget_staff_keys` still blanks only revoked keys.
- **The record (sections 6 and 7).** `staff.js audit-verify` is unchanged; `case_decided`, `appeals_reviewed` and `identity_revealed` are step-up actions, so it refuses a row of them without a valid assertion, and the pinned "nested metadata" vector of this design's tests, a `case_decided` row with no step-up, is now reported with two problems. `staff.js keys` prints, after each account's keys, how many personal accounts are linked to it, never which. The README's staff steps after a restore, which this design's documentation task wrote (section 13), gain a fifth, Moderation.

## 17. Changed by 3f (2026-10-17)

`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-09-authorities-orders-3f-design.md` changes the step-up's actions, the console's width and routes, the staff mails and the console's site.

- **Section 10:** `STAFF_STEP_UP_ACTIONS` gains `order_effected`, `order_event_recorded`, `order_corrected`, `audit_exported` and `gap_closed`; `case_decided`'s action entry gains `reinstate_by_order` with `orderGround`. One `order_effected` row confirms up to ten decisions of one transaction, each named in its metadata; every other action still confirms one.

# korbat sub-project 3c: moderation cases

Date: 2026-10-03. Status: draft r8, written without the user under the standing instruction of 2026-09-23 (keep going; leave only account-dependent steps). The decisions in section 2 were taken here and are flagged for review. Research: `korbat-scratch/research-3c/` (`repo-3c.md`, a map of the code after 3a; `law-3c.md`, the law with its obligations table; `practice-3c.md`, how working systems moderate; `threats-3c.md`, threats T39 to T62 and controls C1 to C40; ten gap answers `gap-G1.md` to `gap-G10.md`, each with lab measurements on PostgreSQL 18.6; and the review records `review-r1.md` to `review-r6.md`), and the earlier `korbat-scratch/research-3/{practice,threats}.md`. ## 1. Context

3a gave staff a console of their own, keys that open it, a step-up that confirms each action with the session's own key, and an audit log that is a hash chain. It gave them nothing to moderate. The trust-and-safety tables of migration 0000 (`cases`, `reports`, `appeals`, `strikes`, `transparency_log`, `packages/db/src/schema/safety.ts:11-96`) have no reader or writer in any app (`repo-3c.md` section 1.7), and they cannot hold what the law now asks: a `reports` row needs a reporter and a rule (`safety.ts:36,39`), so a notice from someone without an account, or about content illegal under a national law but outside R1 to R6, has nowhere to go (Digital Services Act Art. 16, `law-3c.md` section 1). Nothing in the code sets `withheld` or `removed`; every read already honours them (`repo-3c.md` section 2). An author can delete a withheld or removed post and its images today, and an account deletion blanks every post and deletes every image (`apps/api/src/social/repo.ts:480-497,1079-1121`), so the evidence of a case would vanish before anyone decided it.

korbat's promise is that content limits are narrow and public, that every removal cites a public rule, shows the author exactly what happened and can be appealed to a different human, and that there is no silent reach reduction (main design, Context). 3c is where that promise is built or broken. It must also meet the law that binds a micro platform now: Art. 16 notices from anyone, Art. 17 statements of reasons for every restriction, Art. 14 terms that describe the procedure, the TCO Regulation's terrorist-content policy in the terms (`law-3c.md` key findings 1 to 4, 8), Art. 18 and TCO Art. 14(5), which oblige korbat to tell the authorities promptly when it learns of a suspected offence threatening someone's life or safety (met in 3c by the runbook and `staff.js account-facts`; 3e records the notifications, `law-3c.md` 3), and the GDPR for notifiers, reporters and the people reported. And it must not give one or two tired moderators, or someone who stole their key, more power than the record can account for (`threats-3c.md` sections 3.4 and 6).

This design delivers: an intake that takes reports from signed-in users and Art. 16 notices from anyone into one model of intakes and items, merged into one open case per target as a database fact; a queue ordered by severity and age, with no weighting; decisions on posts, single images and profile fields, each carrying a statement of reasons whose every Art. 17(3) element is data, confirmed by the deciding person's staff key without any free text entering the chain; a ledger of measures from which every post's and image's restriction is derived by the database; evidence copied or held at the first report and protected from every destructive path; the author's appeal of a final restriction, reviewed by a different person, which the database enforces, and re-examination of "no action" for notifiers and reporters; the console's queue, case and appeal screens; the app's report form, notice status page and case screens; the mails; the export's moderation section; and the moderation parts of the draft terms and the rulebook.

| Decisions and statements | A decision is the statement of reasons: every Art. 17(3) element is a column (the measures and their durations, the territorial scope, the facts, the source, automation, the legal or contractual ground with its explanation, the redress), in the Transparency Database's shape (`decision_ground`, `category`, `source_type`, the automated flags, a random `puid`) without personal data in any enumerated field, so 3d can publish it (`law-3c.md` 7.3; 6.1). The rulebook is versioned (`RULES_VERSION` 2; version 1 kept) and every decision records the rules and redress versions it was made under, so an old statement renders exactly as sent (practice-3c 11.4); one pure function, `statementParagraphs`, renders it for the author's screen, the console's preview and the mail, so what the moderator previews is what the author gets (practice-3c 10.4; section 10). The statement names the source category only, never a count, a reporter or a report's words (T47). `REDRESS_VERSION` 1 holds three texts: korbat's appeal, for a final restriction; the interim text, for a decision taken while deciding; and the text for a decision its author cannot appeal (section 10); 3e adds an order's. The author is told, in the app at once and by mail, of every decision that restricts, reverses, or ends or lifts a measure taken while deciding, and of every review (6.2 step 10); an interim measure on a target already deleted, which can never take effect, is recorded without a mail. Legal-ground restrictions state their territorial scope as "everywhere": korbat cannot restrict by country (`law-3c.md` 1.5 option (ii)). Flagged: telling authors of no-action decisions (T46 suggests it for legal-ground notices) was not adopted, because it would tell them that someone reported them. Flagged: worldwide scope is more restrictive than a single state's law requires, and the statement says so. Flagged for counsel: whether a final decision on content its author had already deleted is mailed to them; Art. 17 does not require it, and the mail discloses that a report arrived and may tip off a suspect in an Art. 18 case; 3c mails it. | A free `public_reason` text only; rendering old statements with the current rule (Mastodon's flaw); storing every rendered statement as text (personal text kept twice, and the versions make re-rendering exact). |
| Free text under the step-up | G1's option (a), "draft first, then confirm". Every free text a decision, a review or a reveal carries is saved first, without a step-up, into the erasable table `staff_texts`, salted and digested by the console; the server refuses, never changes, a malformed text or one that quotes the case's reports, notices, re-examinations or appeal statements (C19; 7.4). The confirming params carry only ids, enums, integers and digests, so 3a's step-up, `checkStepUpOptions`, `audit-verify` and the chain's canonical text do not change, and the chain never holds readable personal text (T56); erasure nulls the text and keeps the digest; snapshots get a salted digest made by the server at capture. Three writing staff routes therefore stand without a step-up, by name: saving a text, taking a fresh snapshot, and opening a case on the moderator's own finding; none changes anything a user sees (a saved `seal_declined` text ends an urgent repeat and is listed on the home screen, 7.12), and each enters the record only through a confirmed decision that names its digest or its case. Opening a finding still has lasting effects (holds, possibly lane 0; citing R2, it freezes what its case reaches (6.1, the freeze) and makes the final decision an admin's), so findings are limited per staff account and UTC day and listed on the home screen (7.1, 7.3). Flagged: the three exceptions to 3a's rule that every changing staff route asks for the key (3a section 2, Confirming an action); a route-table test lists them. | G1's option (b), the text beside the params (it changes 3a's "the body is the params" rule and wastes a key touch on every refused text); option (c), the text in the params (unerasable for ever, T56); unsalted digests (a short reason or a guessed address could be confirmed by hashing guesses, EDPB Guidelines 02/2025 para 52). |
| The confirmed transaction on the API pool | G2's design: a migrator-owned definer function, `append_confirmed_audit`, EXECUTE to `korbat_api` only, is the last statement of every 3c step-up transaction, so nothing commits after a revocation, a take-down or the challenge's expiry (6.2; G2 measured in section 3). The lock-wait bound moves to `apps/api/src/lib/lock-bounds.ts`, shared by the auth module, the command line and the moderation module (7.5); it only aims to end the transaction before the expiry, which the function itself guarantees. `korbat_api` keeps no USAGE on `auth` (`0001_grants.sql:4`). Flagged: `korbat_api` gains the power to hold a staff account's row `FOR SHARE` for as long as it keeps a transaction open, which can stall `staff.js revoke` until its 10-second timeout, the class of stall 3a already accepts for the audit head (G2 3.6). | An auth-pool transaction around the API-pool one (two connections per decision, a wait the deadlock detector cannot see, G2 4.5); `GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA auth TO korbat_api` (undoes 0001 and makes "revoke PUBLIC on every auth function" a standing rule). |
| No moderation state without a decision | A post's and an image's restriction is never set; the database derives it (P1). Every measure and every reversal is a row of the append-only ledger `decision_actions`, inserted only in the transaction of its own confirmed decision, which the audit link binds to a staff key (6.2). A measure is in force while no row reverses it and, for an interim measure, while its case is open, so interim measures end by themselves when the case's final decision closes it (a seal taken while deciding ends with an admin's answer to the suspect items instead, 6.1 `measures_in_force`). One migrator-owned function, `moderation_apply`, is the only writer of the moderation columns: under the post's lock it takes the strongest measure in force over every case, and under the image rows' locks each image's state (6.2). The result does not depend on the order in which cases, measures and reversals arrive, no case's effect reasons about another's, a new kind of measure only joins the maximum, and an auditor can recompute it (`staff.js text-verify` does). No reversal writes content. A plain trigger on `posts` and column grants keep every other writer off (6.1). Flagged (owner): a lifted or ended field reset does not give the old value back. The person types it again and, when korbat still keeps the case's copy at that moment, reads it on the screen of the decision that reset it for at least 30 days (6.4, 6.6), unless an R4 redaction erased it first. A lift after the copy was erased (a correction after the restriction became final, or after an R4 redaction of the account) finds none, and its statement then makes no such promise (section 10). Keeping the resetting decision's snapshot for as long as a final reset stands was not adopted: it would keep content found to break a rule, for a lift that may never come (GDPR 5(1)(c), (e); P8). Flagged: the 18 places in 7 test files that set a post's state directly (G4 6) move to a fixture that makes a real confirmed decision. | r4's imperative effects, in which each trigger moved `posts.state` and a restore moved a post back only from the state the reversed action set and only when no other removal stood: every round found an ordering of cases, reversals and states the effects missed, the source of most high findings of rounds 2 to 4 (r2-14, r3-9, r3-33, r4-8, r4-14; class C1); G4's deferred "xact" guard on `posts` (it proved only that a matching row was inserted, and needed a time pairing against logical restores, r1-19); G4's `case_events` table (decisions and their actions already are the audited events); case events as `audit_log` rows (a second large index and every event inside the head's lock, G4 4); a second chain head (3,510 deadlocks in 20 s once one path took the heads in the other order, G4 3). |
| Lock order | One order for every transaction that touches moderation: profile rows first (sorted by id, each in the strongest mode the transaction will need), then cases (in their targets' order), then, inside a decision's triggers, the deciding account's and the subject's `auth.users` rows `FOR SHARE` and the cap's advisory lock, then the case's own post, then image rows in id order, then inserts, the audit row and the deferred checks (6.2). A decision locks the subject's profile `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` first, so two decisions about one account serialise; the `FOR KEY SHARE` of likes and follows (`lockLive`, `apps/api/src/social/repo.ts:1160-1163`) never waits for it, and a follow of the subject, a post by the subject or a like of the decided post waits only at its counter update (`repo.ts:609`, `471`, `539`), with no cycle. The author's deletion of a top-level post, which today updates the post and then the profile's `post_count` (`repo.ts:480-497`), takes the profile first (G5 4.2: that one change removed every deletion cycle). An intake takes its cases in their targets' order, then its post targets `FOR SHARE` in id order, then every image row it reaches in one global id order `FOR KEY SHARE` (7.1); it never locks a post it reaches only through an account. The R4 redaction takes the case, then the post, then the post's images in id order (6.4). A seal takes image rows only, in id order; no decision locks a post other than its own case's (6.2). The author's deletion and the purge delete image rows in id order, as `dropDisposable` does (7.10), so nothing locks image rows in another order than an intake that reaches them through an account, which takes no lock on their posts. Flagged: the account purge still updates posts before other accounts' profiles (G5 4.3); a decision that meets it rarely deadlocks, and the decision's one retry covers it. The purge takes its own posts in id order (7.10). Flagged: the intake, the redaction, a seal and a closing decision against `moderation_apply` are measured in the contention lab (section 12). Flagged (owner): measured under load (section 3, lab `lab-gate-k`), the purge of an account with 5,000 image rows takes 2 to 4 s and with 20,000 rows 7 to 16 s, the keep trigger reading the freeze once for each row, and an account's seal takes 1.5 s at 5,000 image rows and 5.9 s at 20,000. Task 2's lab measures both again on a quiet machine. | C8's "case, post, profile" (it deadlocked with likes and replies, G5); taking `FOR UPDATE` on the profile (blocks every like and follow of the account for the decision's length; 3e needs it for suspensions, G5). |
| Recusal and who may decide | A staff account cannot decide where it is a party (the case's subject and the signed-in reporters of the items the decision considers) or where a personal account the operator linked to it (`staff.js link`, `auth.staff_personal_accounts`, readable by no API role) is a party or acted towards one: follows, blocks, mutes, a reply in the last 90 days, or the judged post replying to or quoting it (C27, Wikipedia's "involved" rule, practice-3c 2.7). Only the linked account's own acts count, since anyone can follow or reply to a staff member's posting account alone. The same check on the case's subject refuses opening a case, its images, snapshots and texts, and every reveal in it, and it does not look at reporters, so a refused read says nothing about who reported (6.2 `staff_case_conflict`; 7.3). No final decision may restrict a staff account (`staff_target`, G5 6): staff are disciplined by demotion through grant-role, while an interim measure applies to them as to anyone, so a threat posted from a staff account stops being public at once, and images on a staff account's posts that are reported as child sexual abuse material can be sealed while deciding. Whether a decision needs an admin is a stored fact, `decisions.needs_admin`, forced by the triggers and read by everything that asks (P4; 6.2 step 6, `decision_actions_check`): final decisions that answer a suspect item (6.1, the freeze) or consider an item citing R5, or that cite R2 or R5; every lifting of a seal; corrections of such decisions; and reviews of a decision that sealed images or cites R2 (`review_needs_admin`, 6.3), a review of an R5 restriction staying any eligible moderator's (round 1 decision 11). Interim decisions never need one, so whoever is on duty can seal reported images and withhold a threat while the admin is away, and anyone eligible may lift a measure taken while deciding, except a seal, which only an admin lifts (7.7). Flagged (owner): "senior" becomes "admin"; with one admin, final R2 and R5 decisions and every answer to a suspect item wait for them. Flagged (owner): the first seal is taken while deciding, by any moderator, on a report nobody can check, and hides the images from their author too (r7 showed a post withheld while deciding to its author). Its author cannot appeal it. It lasts until an admin who is not a party answers: with one admin, days, and with that admin recused, without limit; the queue-age mail counts it after 24 hours. The owner may choose r7's form, in which the author loses sight only when an admin seals for good; korbat then serves a file reported as child sexual abuse material to its uploader for as long as the admin is away. Flagged (owner): one moderator's decision while deciding seals every image of an account, also on a finding that moderator opened, and only an admin lifts it. In r7 such a decision hid one post. The decision caps allow 60 decisions an hour; the home screen lists every seal taken while deciding that is in force (7.3). Flagged (owner): reviews inheriting every `needs_admin` (R5 included) was proposed and not adopted, because with one admin those appeals would wait for good (T60); the owner may choose it. Flagged: no "obvious case" exception for a recused moderator (practice-3c 10.20 allows one with a recorded justification); with one moderator the case waits. Flagged: the link names a staff member's posting account inside the auth schema; an API under an attacker's control can still test whether an account is linked or close to one (section 11). | A device-hash comparison between parties and staff (a linkage fact about staff and users, T48's optional item); trusting staff to recuse themselves; computing the admin requirement at each check from the case's composition and from history across cases (r2-13, r3-17). |
| Evidence | Text by copy, images by reference (G6). The first report, notice or finding on a target, and every fresh snapshot, copies the post's or profile's content into an append-only snapshot with a server-made salt and digest, under the post's `FOR SHARE` lock, so an author's deletion comes after it or leaves a tombstone the copy records (G6 E3c); a capture of erased content copies none of it (6.1, T52). Images are held on their own row, which every delete path skips (G6 E3 to E5b); the images and the snapshots of a frozen post are kept by two gates of their own, whatever case holds them and whether a hold stands or not (6.1, the freeze; the keep trigger measured on PostgreSQL 18.6, section 3); one disposal predicate deletes what nothing retains (7.9). The decision names the snapshot and the digest the console computed from what it displayed (T52). Retention follows each kind of data's own users (P8, 6.4, 6.6). Flagged: the snapshot's digest enters the chain only with the decision that names it, not at capture (an intake by anyone would otherwise write a chained row, and an API compromised before the report can forge consistently anyway). Flagged (owner): snapshots of a no-action case go about a day after it closes instead of six months after the notifiers' release (a privacy gain, published in the terms), so a re-examination judges the target as it then stands, and an intake's texts may outlive their case's snapshots by up to six months and 30 days. Flagged (owner): a report or finding of child sexual abuse material, a false one included, keeps every image its case reaches that its author deletes meanwhile, those of a purged account included, unserved, until an admin answers (T41). Flagged: a suspect item about an account copies the account's fields, not its posts' texts. The body of a post its author deletes afterwards is lost unless some case had copied it; the alt texts stay on the kept rows. Flagged for counsel: rows 2, 4, 7, 10, 11, 15 and 17 (backups) of G6's table, and: how long korbat may and must keep sealed images, and on what basis, given that 3c's software has no function to erase them (Directive 2011/93/EU Art. 5 and recital 17; national law); on which basis it keeps, on an unverified report, images their author deleted and the images of a purged account until an admin answers, and the snapshots of a frozen post in other cases past their own periods (GDPR Art. 5(1)(e), 6(1)(c) or (f), 17(3)(b) or (e)); that an account case's own evidence goes by its ordinary due rules after a seal for good while the images are kept; and whether korbat may keep the account facts it printed for a report to the police until the admin answers. Flagged (owner): backups are deleted 30 days after they were taken (`RETENTION.backupDays`, 6.6), a period the terms publish and sub-project 4's backup job must keep. | Snapshots of media ids alone (the files are swept within the hour, G6 E1); copying image files (a new worker protocol, disk); keeping evidence only for decided cases (the author deletes first, T18); a foreign key from evidence to the image row (it made the author's deletion fail, G6); a separate holds table (it left holds pointing at nothing, G6); one case-wide due time over every decision, appeal, item and mail of a case and its intakes' other cases (r4's `moderation_due`, which gained a term for each late path and still made evidence due too early or never, r3-22, r4-17; class C7). |
| What the author sees of removed content | Ordinary removals (R1, R3, R5, R6, and the law): the author keeps seeing the body and images in their own view and export while they keep the post (main design line 191: never silently gone; GDPR Art. 15(3)). R4: as written until the restriction is final (for a frozen post, until the freeze ends), then redacted (6.4), with the chip "Removed: R4" and "Content erased when the R4 decision became final" on the decision screens (Art. 15(4), EDPB 01/2022 paras 172-173). Images reported as child sexual abuse material: once sealed (6.2), from the first seal taken while deciding, they reach no reader, their author included (Directive 2011/93/EU Art. 5(5)): each is a placeholder in every view, "Sealed: not shown to anyone, you included" for its author and the placeholder of a hidden image for anyone else, and the export holds none of them (7.10, 7.11). Text is never sealed: the post keeps its text and its place in its author's views and export, and a text that itself breaks a rule is restricted by the ordinary measures under that rule, which leave it with its author as any removal does. A withheld or removed image goes to its author with its state and to others as a placeholder that does not say which; a sealed one, and one an R4 redaction erased, to nobody. Flagged (owner): text is never sealed. The author of a post whose images are sealed keeps seeing its text, and so do others, unless a moderator restricts the post under a rule or the law (the runbook says to withhold the post as well when its text links to or offers such material); r7's hidden sealed post and its amendment of main design line 191 are withdrawn. Flagged (owner): others see "Image hidden by korbat moderation" on each sealed image of a post that stays public; after an account's seal that is every image post of the profile. r7's withhold while deciding took the post out of others' sight without a mark. Flagged for counsel: Directive 2011/93/EU Art. 2(c) defines the material as visual (read 2026-10-03), but it sets a minimum. Counsel says whether the home Member State's law counts words (a written depiction, instructions) as such material, and what the recast's adopted definition says; a summary of the Commission's proposal has it cover instructions whatever their form. If words can be the material, a text removed under R2 cannot stay in its author's view and export, and the seal needs a form for text; that an author may keep their own words is this design's reading. Flagged for counsel: the author's own sealed images are left out of the export and of an access answer on a report nobody checked (GDPR Art. 15(3) and 20): on which basis (Art. 15(4), Art. 23 and national law), and what the answer says; korbat's copy may be the only one. Flagged for counsel: the R4 redaction of a frozen post waits for the admin's answer, so a doxxed address there outlives the restriction's finality until then. Flagged for counsel: whether removed R3 or R5 bodies naming a third person may stay with their author without end (G6 row 2). | Hiding every removed post's content from its author (breaks "never silently gone"); serving sealed images to their uploader (making them available); sealing the post with its text, as r7 did (a post state every reader of text had to learn, snapshots withheld from the staff who had just read them, captures without content, an export rule, and a report to the police that had to be written before the seal because nothing showed the text afterwards; the Directive's definition is visual). |
| Deletion and cases | The author's deletion and the purge write only lifecycle columns and the author's own content, and delete only image rows nothing retains; they never write a moderation column or row. Moderation never writes a lifecycle column: on the one shared column, `posts.state`, deletion only moves it to `deleted_by_author` and moderation never moves it to or from that value, for every role (6.1 `posts_guard`). Moderation writes content only two ways, each one-way: a field reset at its decision (nothing on a deleted profile) and the R4 redaction (6.4). So cases about deleted targets go on and are decided on their snapshots, measures on them are recorded and in force, nothing writes into a row the purge anonymised, and the redaction acts whatever the post's lifecycle (P3). Liveness is one rule for every route (7.1 step 3): a suspect item's target is live while its row exists, a deleted post and a purged account included, so no report of child sexual abuse material about anything that exists is answered automatically, an account also under a handle it has left, which `handle_history` keeps reserved for it; for every other ground a deleted post or account is a target with nothing live. While a post is frozen, no delete path takes its images and no erasure its snapshots (6.1, the freeze). The retention job's `dropDisposable` is the one deleter of images a case kept: its predicate chooses the candidates (7.9), and gate K (`post_media_keep`) decides for every delete (6.1, the freeze). Flagged (owner): a report of child sexual abuse material about a post its author deleted, or about a purged account, is not answered automatically: it waits for an admin, and what is left of the post's images is kept until then (T41: a false report can keep deleted images that long, and costs an admin a decision). Flagged (owner): deletion no longer stops a case from producing a decision. | A deleted post with a held image live for every ground (repeated reports would keep content its author deleted and put deleted images before staff for no protective purpose, T41, GDPR 5(1)(e)); r7's liveness for this path, which read whether an image was still held and so needed an exception for each way a deleted post could still show images (r6-1, r6-3); liveness from `posts.state` with a ground-keyed exception (r4-1, r4-3); reversals that write content back into deleted or anonymised rows (r1-33, r2-24, r4-7); four image deleters (r1-10, r2-22; class C4). |
| Suspected child sexual abuse material | Nobody at korbat opens it. The mechanics are stated once, in 6.1 (the freeze) and 6.2 (the seal); this row gives the decision and its flags. A report on the CSAM path, or a moderator's finding citing R2, is a **suspect item**. While it is unanswered, every post its case reaches is **frozen**: a post case reaches its post, an account case every post of the account, and a report about a post that quotes another is taken in as two items, one for each post, so no case reaches another author's post. Frozen means three things, each enforced at one gate that every path of its kind must pass: no image row of the post is deleted and no file of it requested (a trigger), no snapshot of it is erased (the one function that erases snapshots), and no staff member is served its images, on any case, open or closed (the one function that opens an image for staff). A report hides nothing by itself. A person does, with one measure, the **seal**: it seals every image the case reaches, for everyone, their author included; whoever is on duty takes it while deciding, and an admin takes it for good or answers without it. Only images are sealed, never text. Every suspect item about something that exists waits for an admin, who answers all suspect items of a case at once, and only an admin lifts a seal, a seal for good only on the answer of the authority the images were reported to (6.2, the seal; 7.7). On a seal for good the operator reports to the national police or the authority its Member State names, never to a hotline, whose analyst assesses what an address shows while a sealed image answers 404 to everyone (`research-3/practice.md` INHOPE paragraph), and an admin seals for good only what korbat then reports (runbook, Task 12(a)). Every staff account is mailed at once after a decision that lifts a seal or answers a suspect item without one, and the home screen lists them for 30 days, as for reveals (7.5 step 4, 7.12). 3c keeps what it sealed: the release, the quarantine and the replay after a restore are 3d's, and the record of the report to the authority is 3e's (sections 16, 17). Flagged (owner): a report of child sexual abuse material hides nothing by itself. From the report until a staff member seals the images while deciding they stay public: for as long as it takes one of one or two people to read a mail, hours at night, a day or more when both are away. The urgent mail, repeated about every 20 minutes, is the only alert until 3e's phone alert, and lane 0's target is 24 hours. After a seal, Cloudflare's edge and browsers may still serve a copy for up to five minutes, until 3d's purge. Until the seal only the rule that staff never open a reported post in the app keeps them from seeing it, and after it the app still shows what the case does not reach. The person who seals cannot look: here "a person decides" means that a person may refuse, in a flood or on a plain repeat, and acts under a name, a key, a record and the caps. What shrinks the window without a program deciding on a report is 3e's phone alert and 3d's hash match, both before sub-project 4. Flagged (owner): the seal on an account case covers every image on the account's posts, because nobody can tell which ones the report means. So one anonymous report that names an account, and that nobody can check, can hide every image the account ever posted from everyone, its author included; the report form asks for the post or the image instead where the sender can give it (section 9). An admin who can tell from the report's words which post is meant opens a finding on that post instead and answers the account's item without a seal. The account's notifier then reads its answer with `ACCOUNT_SUSPECT_SCOPE`, and the statement of the finding's seal names a moderator's finding as its source. Flagged for counsel: whether Art. 17(3)(b) needs that statement to say that it followed a notice. Flagged (owner): a seal covers the images that exist when it is taken. Until 3e's suspension an account whose images are sealed can post new ones; while its item is unanswered they are frozen and the urgent mail starts again, after a recorded choice not to seal as after a seal (7.12), and after the answer they need a report of their own. Flagged (owner): a report of this kind about a post that quotes another opens a case on the quoted post too, in the urgent lane, so that author's images are frozen, and may be sealed, on a report that named someone else's post; the notifier may have meant the quoting post's own images. An added item does not count against a notice's ten targets, so a notice of ten quoting posts opens twenty urgent cases. Flagged (owner): after an admin's answer without a seal, moderators may open the images (as round 2 decision 21 allowed for a closed case), and every staff account is mailed. That answer is, in effect, the decision that staff may now look: the first person who opens an image afterwards is the first to learn what it is. Flagged (owner): 3c's software has no function to release, hand over or erase sealed images; it keeps them, and the operator does either by hand on an authority's written instruction (runbook). korbat does not meet people the operator does not know before 3e and 3d have shipped (row Splitting 3c).
